prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned prose and poetry that build from memory, the body and dream an inner cosmos of metaphysical scope.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B050, one writer, one prize part. I reached it on the common criteria, and the round-1 exchange has not changed the merit reasons. The chair's summary records that all six files name the same writer. I do not treat that as evidence of merit, and it is not part of my reasoning. As publicly described, Cărtărescu's voice is among the most distinctive on the shortlist. In Blinding (the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid, memory, the body and dream are built into a sustained metaphysical project, with a formal architecture that appears to hold across volumes. The poetic origin and the essays suggest the claim covers an authorship, not one celebrated book. I take the chair's question about which works each member relies on seriously. My claim rests mainly on the large prose, on public knowledge of Blinding and Solenoid. My confidence about the poetry, essays and early prose is lower. If the committee words the citation, I would lead with the prose and treat the poetic foundation as supporting breadth, not as an independent pillar. I keep Tawada (B018) and Zurita (B009) as alternatives because each makes a different, serious literary claim: Tawada for linguistic and formal invention between Japanese and German, Zurita for a sustained poetic sequence. On the chair's last question, I see no merit reason to prefer no award (P000). The open questions concern what the committee should specify and verify. They are not grounds to withhold a prize from an oeuvre of this scale and distinctiveness.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unresolved and goes to the sustained-quality criterion. The late, very large volumes may deepen the earlier project, or they may enlarge it and repeat its motifs. My knowledge comes from public description and translation, not close reading, and I cannot settle this. The density and rhythm of the Romanian prose may survive only partly in translation. Coverage of the poetry and early work is thinner than of the major novels, so the whole-oeuvre claim is partly inferred. If the committee's Romanian readers found that the late books circle the early ones, the case would narrow to the major cycles, and I would reopen the comparison with B018 and B009. I also accept that my second-tier ordering is weakly grounded. I rated Zurita seventh in my opening ranking and now name him an alternative, and I am less sure of my knowledge of Tawada's full corpus than my ranking implied.

responses.point: Olsson moved from Zurita first and Cărtărescu second in his opening ranking to Cărtărescu first in round 1, keeping B009 as first alternative and B018 as second. He says my caution about scope moved him, that Zurita's recurrence depends on a narrower generic range than Cărtărescu's, and that he shares my doubt about whether Tawada's short, episodic forms give enough sustained depth.
responses.response: I note his disclosure of the shift and I weigh his stated reasons, not the shift itself. I agree his wording for Zurita must stay strictly with the written sequences, and on that point my round-1 reservation and his coincide. I am less convinced that a narrower generic range makes recurrence more damaging for Zurita. A single sequential project can deepen by revisiting its own forms, and I cannot show from translation that it does not. What I can say is that we cannot tell without naming individual poems in the sequences and testing them. On Tawada, the chair asked what evidence would show that her shorter forms sustain depth. My answer is as follows. The representative works listed for her include novels (The Emissary, Memoirs of a Polar Bear), so I should not call her work only short or episodic. The question is cumulative. It asks whether the Japanese-language and German-language bodies of work, with the essays and drama, develop a formal problem over time or restate one device. That needs readers of both languages, and I do not claim to be one.

responses.point: Mattson said she would revisit Tawada if readers of both languages can show depth across the corpus. She also said Cărtărescu's project is built on language and consciousness at an architectural scale that Tawada's does not attempt, and that she reads his recurring motifs as the architecture of a personal mythology and not as mere repetition.
responses.response: I accept the offer to revisit and would accept the same condition for myself. I would qualify the scale argument. Architectural scale is one form of formal ambition, but it is not itself a criterion. A writer who makes estrangement between two languages into a method works at a different scale and may still show comparable invention. So I prefer Cărtărescu because his project looks to me more sustained and more fully realised, not because it is bigger. On the personal-mythology reading, I find it plausible and I do not exclude it, but it is exactly what is untested. A mythology that deepens would show a formal problem posed in one book and posed differently in a later one. A mythology that repeats would restate it. That is a question the committee can put to the texts. On NDiaye, whom the chair asks you to defend by named works, I remain where I was: a credible later-round option, not above B050 for me.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg keeps B050 first but states that wide agreement in the opening rankings is not evidence of merit. He also says the committee should test directly whether the very large late volumes are self-enclosed or repetitive, and that he now treats Zurita (B009) as an alternative, provided the poems are compared and not the scale of the project.
responses.response: I agree on both points and want to make the test operational. For Cărtărescu I would ask the Romanian readers whether the later volumes reframe the earlier material or only reproduce it. For Zurita I accept his proposal to compare individual poems, because it addresses my own worry about how the citation would be worded. I would add one limit that he shares. The committee should not take uniform support for B050 as a reason to skip this test. If we agree on a name before we have tested its main weakness, the agreement does not strengthen the case. I would also ask him to say what specific late work he thinks extends the early project, as opposed to the general description. The profile of the late work I rely on is public and general, and I have no better evidence than that.

responses.point: Carlberg argues that Cărtărescu's architecture (recurring images, long structural design) survives translation better than the sonic and positional effects of poetry, and that the committee should say which volumes it is relying on. She also notes that I raised the question of Tawada's sustained depth myself.
responses.response: I agree that the committee should name its volumes, and I have done so above. I would qualify the translation argument. Structural design may survive rendering, but the rhythm and syntax that Carlberg herself says define the effect of Cărtărescu's prose are what translation tends to flatten. So the asymmetry between prose and poetry is real but partial, and it should not become a reason to rank prose above poetry by default. It is a reason for caution about the poetry candidates, and I treat it that way for Zurita and Adonis. On Tawada, she is right that I raised the doubt and I stand by it. The doubt does not decide the question. Her bilingual position complicates translation loss, since part of the work was written in German, and that may make parts of her corpus easier for the committee to read in the original than the Romanian or Spanish candidates. I cannot say how far that is true, so I leave it as a question for the committee.

uncertainties: Translation: how much of the density, rhythm and syntax of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose survives in the translations the committee uses, and how much weaker the translated coverage is for the poetry and essays.

Whether the late, very large volumes deepen the earlier project or repeat its motifs. I cannot settle this without close reading of the whole corpus, and no round-1 file offers verified close-reading evidence on either side.

Corpus coverage for the alternatives: how fully the Japanese and German bodies of work by Tawada, taken together with her essays and drama, show sustained depth, and whether I am underweighting less translated work.
Whether Zurita's written sequences carry the case on their own in Spanish, apart from the landscape-scale and memorial interventions and the historical occasion.

All judgments rest on public knowledge of representative works, not fresh reading or independent verification of texts or critical consensus. My comparisons with candidates I ranked lower (Michon, NDiaye, Adonis, Yan Lianke, Alexis Wright, Mia Couto) are the least secure.
Carlberg's committee voting status is undocumented and her simulated vote is a modeling assumption. This simulation models a committee recommendation, not the decision of the full Swedish Academy.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. None apparent from the supplied profile. The only listed connections are shared committee and Academy membership with colleagues and programme engagement with Swedish cultural bodies, and none ties me to a shortlisted writer. My own practice as a novelist is context, not evidence of preference. I disclose that I ranked Zurita seventh in my opening ranking and now list him as an alternative, and that I take his case more seriously after the exchange, for the stated reasons about the written sequences.
